text: You get two sorted arrays, nums1 of size m and nums2 of size n. Return the median of the two arrays combined. The run time has to be log of m plus n.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — that last line is the whole problem. Without it, I'd merge the two arrays and grab the middle. The log requirement means I'm not allowed to touch every element; even one pass is too slow. Can either array be empty?
Yes, either one can be empty, but not both — m plus n is at least one. Both are at most a thousand long, and values fit in plus or minus ten to the sixth.

Good, I'll come back to that value range — it matters more than it looks. Let me think about what a median actually is for a sec. A median isn't really a number. It's a place where you cut. You split all the data into two halves of nearly equal size, with everything on the left at most everything on the right, and read the median off the values next to the cut. So don't hunt for the number — hunt for the cut. A cut has a position, which is a single number I can binary search on. On the example, one, three and two: three items, so the median is the second smallest, two. If the left half is one, two and the right is three, the median is the largest thing on the left.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would merge both arrays and index the middle. That's linear time and space — correct, but exactly what the requirement forbids. A better one finds the k-th smallest recursively, throwing away half of k each time. That does hit log time, but it has a lot of edge cases: one side running short, the k equals one base case, and calling it twice when the total is even. This problem reminds me of binary searching a partition rather than a value. I know how many items the left half must hold — call it leftCount. So if nums1 contributes i items, nums2 contributes leftCount minus i, automatically. Two unknowns collapse into one, and one unknown with a too-big or too-small test is exactly a binary search.

Here's the plan. One: swap so nums1 is the shorter array, and set leftCount to m plus n plus one, over two — the plus one puts the spare item on the left when the total is odd. Two: binary search i, the items nums1 gives the left half, with j equal to leftCount minus i, and read the four values around the cut. Three: the cut is legal when L1 is at most R2 and L2 is at most R1; within one array that order is free, since it's sorted. If L1 is bigger than R2, nums1 gave too many; if L2 is bigger than R1, too few. Both can't fail at once, so the branches never conflict. One thing worth flagging: the swap isn't just for speed — it's what keeps j in bounds. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. After the swap and leftCount, it's a binary search on i: compute j, read the four neighbors, then move hi, move lo, or return — the max of the left side for an odd total, or its average with the min of the right side for an even one. One thing worth flagging is the sentinels. At an edge I use int min or int max, so they always lose inside max and min. Could the even branch add int min plus int max? No — that needs an empty left half or an empty right half, and neither is possible. I also measured it: the largest sum was two times ten to the sixth.

Let's dry-run the code with one, three, five, thirteen, twenty-five and six, twelve, fifteen, eighteen, twenty-one; leftCount is five. Round one gives too few, round two too many. Round three is the one to look at: the left half is one, three, five plus six, twelve, and both crosswise checks pass. The total is even, so I average twelve and thirteen — twelve point five. That matches merging by hand. Corner cases: one, three and two gives two, from the odd branch. One, two and three, four gives two point five, with both sentinels. An empty array with one, two gives one point five. A thousand copies each of minus and plus ten to the sixth gives zero.

The time complexity is log of the smaller length — better than the log of m plus n that was asked, because I search only the shorter array. Space is constant; the recursion goes at most one level deep, since after the swap m is at most n. In the worst case both arrays are a thousand long, so the loop runs about ten times. The loop is lo at most hi with a return inside, because as i grows the states go too few, legal, too many — I want the middle stretch, not a boundary. Oh, one more thing — the sentinel trick borrows two values out of the range. It's safe only because values are capped at ten to the sixth. If values could span the whole int range, the addition overflows, and I'd make the sentinels and the four locals long long.

That's a strong answer. Three things stood out. You reframed the problem before reaching for a technique — a median is a cut, not a number — and then noticed the cut has only one free variable once the left-half size is fixed. You corrected the usual story about the swap: most candidates say it's for speed; you showed it's what keeps j in bounds, which makes it a correctness requirement. And on the overflow question you gave me a proof and then backed it with a measurement. Knowing that a clean argument isn't the same as evidence is exactly what I want to see.
